JSON: Name: organic_innovation_attitudes_survey Title: Comparative quantitative analysis using stratified survey sampling and multivariate statistical modeling of stakeholder acceptance of innovations in organic farming Short Hypothesis: Controlling for farm size, age, and education, membership in an organic certification association is associated with lower acceptance of genetic-engineering-based breeding methods (e.g., CRISPR/Cas and hybrid breeding) compared with non-member farmers. Related Work: Prior work identifies three intersecting themes relevant to innovation acceptance in organic farming: (1) normative principles of organic systems (naturalness, closed nutrient cycles) which drive resistance to certain technologies; (2) technical and digital tools (precision agriculture, robotics) that promise efficiency gains but face cost, complexity and acceptability barriers in organic contexts; and (3) social innovations (networking, value-chain arrangements, participatory breeding) that increase uptake and legitimacy. Existing quantitative studies are limited in scale, frequently non-representative, and often report descriptive group differences without multivariate controls or causal analysis. Qualitative and small-sample studies report attitude–behavior gaps and context sensitivity, while policy reviews highlight contested trade-offs (yields vs biodiversity; openness to technology vs integrity). Shortcomings in the literature include sparse stratified comparisons across stakeholder classes (conventional farmers, organic EU-certified, organic association members, advisors, processors, consumers), limited use of mediation/moderation modeling to test underlying mechanisms (e.g., naturalness as mediator), lack of behavioral validation (purchase or seed-use data), and inadequate power to estimate subgroup effects and interactions. Abstract: This study addresses how distinct stakeholder groups evaluate innovations and development strategies for organic farming, focusing on genetic breeding methods, technical/digital tools, and social/value-chain innovations. We propose a stratified survey of stakeholders (conventional farmers, EU-certified organic farms, organic-association members, advisors, processors, and consumers) coupled with multivariate statistical modeling to quantify predictors of acceptance and perceived development potential. Main methods include ordinal logistic regression, mixed-effects models, mediation and moderation analysis, and latent class clustering to identify attitude typologies. The primary contribution is a robust, controlled quantification of the association between organizational membership and rejection of specific innovation types, and a typology of stakeholder segments that differ in priorities (climate adaptation, biodiversity, yields, digitalization). Expected outcomes are (1) effect-size estimates for key predictors of acceptance, (2) evidence about whether 'naturalness' mediates rejection of genetic breeding methods, and (3) an empirically grounded mapping of development pathways that can inform research prioritization and policy design. Experiments: Dataset: primary cross-sectional survey administered to a stratified sample (target N=1000) with strata: conventional farmers (CF, n=250), EU-certified organic farmers (EU-OF, n=250), organic association members (OF-assoc, n=250), advisors/processors/retailers (n=125), and consumers/interested public (n=125). Supplement with administrative farm registry variables (farm size, region) where available. Questionnaire: standard demographic and farm variables; 5-point Likert items on importance/acceptance for listed innovations (CRISPR/Cas, hybrid breeding, population-variety breeding, precision farming, agriphotovoltaics, smart farming, mother-bonded calf rearing, network platforms); explicit 'should not be used' option; psychometric scales for naturalness orientation and innovation openness; behavioral validation items (self-reported recent seed/purchase choices). Preprocessing: remove responses failing attention checks; multiple imputation for item-missingness if <20% per respondent; otherwise exclude. Baselines: descriptive replication of original fair study; unadjusted group comparisons (Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney U) on acceptance scores. Primary models: ordinal logistic regression for acceptance of CRISPR/hybrid breeding with predictors: association membership (binary), farm type, farm size, age, education, naturalness scale, region; report odds ratios, 95% CI, and marginal effects. Mixed-effects models: include random intercepts for region and survey mode. Mediation analysis: test whether naturalness score mediates association membership -> rejection of CRISPR (bootstrap 5,000 samples). Moderation analysis: test farm size and economic reliance on crop income as moderators. Clustering: latent class analysis on innovation-acceptance items to identify attitude segments; compare cluster membership distribution across strata. Predictive validation: train/test split 80/20 for logistic models; report AUC, calibration (Brier score), and cross-validated RMSE for continuous composite acceptance indices. Ablation studies: (A) remove naturalness mediator from model; (B) remove association membership; (C) replace ordinal models with linear models on mean acceptance to compare robustness. Multiple comparisons: control FDR at 5% for tests across innovation items. Power calculation: to detect an odds ratio equivalent to small-to-moderate effect (Cohen's d~0.3) with alpha=0.05 and power=0.8, require ~200 observations per primary comparison group; target N accounts for subgroup analyses. External validation: where possible, correlate latent clusters with self-reported recent seed/technology choices (binary) and compute Cohen's kappa/agreement. Risk Factors and Limitations: Selection bias from fair-based or convenience recruitment leading to overrepresentation of pro-organic or student participants and underrepresentation of conventional farmers; nonresponse and social desirability bias on ethically charged items; measurement error and construct validity limits in single-item innovation acceptance measures; ambiguity in 'should not be used' responses complicating ordinal modeling; confounding and reverse causality in observational data preventing strong causal claims (membership may be endogenous to attitudes); insufficient subgroup sample sizes for some strata leading to low power for interactions; multiple-testing false discovery risk if many innovations are tested without correction; limited external behavioral validation if sales/seed-use records are unavailable; regional specificity to Germany limiting generalizability to other countries and agroecological contexts; potential collinearity among predictors (e.g., association membership correlated with farm size/education) complicating coefficient interpretation; model misspecification risk for ordinal versus continuous treatment of Likert scales.
